national.title: Buying new things feels wonderful. But it can also be a trap
national.summary: Constantly buying new things can be problematic, says journalist Eric Athas, author of the new book "Saying No to New." Here's how to break the cycle and find joy in what you already have.
national.body:
Buyer beware: Holiday shopping season is here. Is every sale calling your name? Is your virtual shopping cart overflowing?

Before you start buying everything, take note. There's a reason new things get us excited, says Eric Athas, author of Saying No to New: Why New Things Are Stealing Your Time, Money, and Happiness — and How to Take Back Your Life , published in September. Our brains are wired to seek out newness, and the retail industry is set up to keep us coming back for more as quickly as possible.

Life Kit Listen to the podcast version of this story That constant consumption of novel possessions — whether they're brand-new, digital, secondhand or even free — can be problematic. "It's hard to be grateful for what you have if you're always on the lookout for something else ," he says.

To break the cycle of chasing newness, we need to shop with more intention and find joy in what we already own, Athas says. In a conversation with Life Kit, he explains how. This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

Our brains are programmed to find new things interesting and old things boring.

If you think about our ancient ancestors, it was beneficial [for their survival] to explore new foods to eat and new territory and eventually explore different parts of the world.

There's also research that shows when we encounter something new, we get a little shot of dopamine. You get that feeling of excitement when you first use that new app or try that new video game or bring home a new gizmo for the kitchen.

New things can steal our happiness. Everyone can relate to the feeling of tearing open that new box or putting on that new outfit. You do feel joy and excitement from that initially.

national.title: A quintessential Route 66 diner has been serving up Americana for nearly 100 years
national.summary: The Ariston Cafe opened its doors in 1924 to serve travelers along Route 66 and has dished up classic American road fare ever since.
national.body:
The Ariston Cafe in Litchfield, Ill., is one of the oldest continuously operating restaurants along Route 66. Neeta Satam for NPR hide caption

The Ariston Cafe along Route 66 in Litchfield, Ill., has been a favorite for more than 90 years. Just past the front door, underneath the vintage neon signs that read "Ariston" and "Budweiser," is a diner staple: a glass case, full of sweet temptations. It took one of the Ariston's owners, Will Law, nearly a full minute to reel off all 12 of the day's choices.

Server Michelle Cordie holds a dessert tray at the Ariston Cafe. Neeta Satam for NPR hide caption

"There's a peach crisp bread pudding with the vanilla bourbon sauce," he said. "Then, of course, a traditional cheesecake with or without cherries, and we have a chocolate delight, a lemon delight, a coconut delight."

They were all delightful to look at and the kind of classic American comfort desserts that you might crave while you're road-tripping on America's most famous highway. All of them — like everything else served at the Ariston — are still made in-house.

Litchfield isn't the most natural stop on Route 66; it's a sleepy town about an hour outside St. Louis. But the Ariston Cafe, which sits just across the road from the charming Litchfield Museum & Route 66 Welcome Center , has become an institution in its own right with its wooden chairs and cozy decor.

The Litchfield Museum & Route 66 Welcome Center celebrates the history of Route 66. Neeta Satam for NPR hide caption

Travelers still flock to the Ariston, thanks to the internet and social media. The waitstaff says many visitors come in already knowing exactly what they intend to order based on what they've read and seen online.

national.title: In a time of rising costs, one Thanksgiving commodity is cheaper: cannabis
national.summary: Steep discounts for "Green Wednesday," one of the highest-selling days for cannabis, help customers keep costs down. But experts say retailers are feeling the pinch.
national.body:
Customers buy products at the Harvest Medical Marijuana Dispensary in San Francisco in 2016. Haven Daley/AP hide caption

This Thanksgiving season, Americans are paying more for almost everything: travel costs have soared, and the price of food has risen . Bringing wine to the family dinner? That costs more, too.

But there's one thing consumers buy at high rates that will actually get cheaper this time of year: marijuana.

Known in the industry as "Green Week" or "Green Wednesday," the days ahead of Thanksgiving have come to rival famed stoner holiday 4/20 as the day cannabis dispensaries see the most sales — and highest foot traffic — of the year.

In most dispensaries around the country, that means steep discounts, doorbuster specials and exclusive products. It's a good deal for customers, who line up in long queues as they await their turn with the so-called budtenders behind the counter.

Cannabis in the U.S. is a $30 billion industry with legal marketplaces in 24 states and the nation's capital, according to Whitney Economics, a firm that specializes in economic research and consulting on the business of cannabis. But in recent years, the deep discounts that have drawn in customers — and kept them coming back for weeks like this one — have squeezed retailers and resulted in a revenue decline in the legal market.

As the week began at The Forest, a dispensary in Baltimore, shoppers were stocking up for the holiday week.

A pack of gummies to bring to Friendsgiving in lieu of alcohol. A sparkling THC-infused beverage for those canna-curious in-laws. Or a holiday staple: some pre-rolls to share on an evening walk.

national.title: Prince William and Kate's country home broken into, 2 arrested
national.summary: Two men were arrested over a suspected burglary at the U.K. royal family's Sandringham Estate, the country residence of Prince William and Catherine, police said.
national.body: Two men have been arrested over a suspected burglary at the royal family's Sandringham Estate, the country residence of William and Catherine, the Prince and Princess of Wales, U.K. police said.Police responded to reports of "suspicious activity" at Anmer Hall on King Charles III's Sandringham estate in eastern England Monday at about 6 p.m., Norfolk police said. William and Catherine and the rest of their family weren't present at the time, the police said.The police said Wednesday that Mirgen Doku, 34, and Arilen Ndoci, 32, were charged with entering a dwelling with intent to steal and trespassing on a protected site. They were due in court later Wednesday. ]Police dogs, drones and a helicopter were used to search the property and make the arrests, officials said. Kensington Palace told CBS News it wouldn't comment on security matters. Anmer Hall, which has 10 bedrooms, was a wedding present to the couple from Queen Elizabeth II. It is used as a country residence on weekends. William and his family spend most of their time at Forest Lodge in Windsor, which they have described as their "forever home." The reported break-in came as William visited Prime Minister Andy Burnham at the British leader's office, 10 Downing Street.Catherine recently opened up about finding hope and joy amid uncertainty in a new documentary exploring life since her cancer diagnosis in 2024."Heal" follows the 44-year-old royal as she attempts the Three Peaks Challenge, climbing the highest mountains in Scotland, England and Wales within 24 hours. The film will premiere on the BBC in the United Kingdom on Nov. 29, before airing internationally on NBCUniversal in the United States on Nov. 30.

national.title: Army to detonate unstable lead explosives at Iowa plant today
national.summary: The U.S. Army will detonate a stockpile of degrading explosives at a munitions plant in Iowa on Wednesday, after days of back-and-forth between politicians and the courts.
national.body: The U.S. Army is set to detonate a stockpile of degrading explosives at a munitions plant in Iowa on Wednesday morning, following community outcry and a legal fight that delayed the operation by several days. Five tons of unstable explosive material, containing the highly sensitive compound lead azide, will be blown up in a controlled detonation at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown at 9 a.m. local time. Middletown is a small community of about 350 people, located four hours west of Chicago by car. The plant houses about 68 barrels or roughly 10,000 pounds of lead azide, which has been used in ammunition since World War I. According to the Environmental Protection Agency, the explosives degraded over about 20 years in storage, giving way to a process called recrystallization that made the material more susceptible to accidental detonation from friction or other movement.The Army has pushed to carry out the controlled detonation because of the public safety risks associated with the cache possibly blowing up on its own. But environmental groups and local residents attempted to block its plans, fearing the health and agricultural consequences of a toxic plume of lead dust that could disperse across the region after the blast. The plume was expected to spread over parts of southeastern Iowa and northeastern Missouri, potentially threatening homes, playgrounds, farmlands and other spaces. Maps released Tuesday by the Army noted that the dust cloud could travel as far as 100 miles, but the most potent effects would likely be felt within 30 square miles of the munitions plant. Legal challenge questioned detonationThe detonation was postponed last week after environmental groups filed a lawsuit challenging the emergency permit the EPA had granted the Army to authorize it. The groups argued the agency had not provided residents of the area with adequate notice of its plans or evidence showing the detonation was the best course of action from a health and safety perspective. But the 8th Circuit Court of Appeals' initial ruling blocking the detonation was lifted Monday. national.summary: Data from the months after Nebraska's early rollout of new Medicaid work mandates offers a look at the challenges enrollees in other states could face.
national.body: When Nebraska chose to implement Medicaid work requirements eight months before it was called for under President Trump's sweeping 2025 budget law, many health policy analysts panned the decision. They worried people would lose coverage because of system glitches.Many also watched the Cornhusker State's experience to see whether it would offer lessons to the more than three dozen other states that would follow it in 2027.On Nov. 13, the Trump administration gave states the option of taking extra time to get ready. They'll have until July 2027, rather than January, to begin dropping coverage for people who don't meet the work requirements. States have until Dec. 11 to decide whether they will still fully implement the requirements on Jan. 1 and begin dropping those who don't comply or start refusing new coverage to people who aren't working.Congressional Democrats, who often criticized Medicaid work requirements on the campaign trail and have sided with states in urging a reprieve from the January deadline, claimed victory. "The Trump-Vance Administration finally admitted what Democrats have said from the very beginning: Republicans' chaotic maze of red tape requirements jeopardize the health care of millions of Americans," Sen. Ron Wyden (D-Ore.) and Rep. Frank Pallone (D-N.J.) said in a statement. Democrats' massive election victories in November will give them control of both chambers of Congress next year. Top Democrats said they'll prioritize legislation to stop the Medicaid work requirements before they're fully enforced.The basicsNot everyone in Medicaid must comply with the new requirements. national.title: Iran denounces U.S. use of AI in war
national.summary: Iran's U.N. envoy claims the U.S. military used Palantir and Anthropic AI systems to select some 2,000 targets over just four days.
national.body: Iran has denounced the U.S. military's use of artificial intelligence to plan and carry out attacks. Speaking at a U.N. Security Council meeting Tuesday, Iranian Ambassador Gholamhossein Darzi said the weaponization of AI "raises serious concerns." Darzi claimed U.S. forces used the technology to deploy more than 2,000 munitions to hit 2,000 distinct targets within 96 hours. He said Palantir's Maven and Anthropic's Claude system were used to analyze intelligence, identify and prioritize targets and provide strike coordinates. "Neither advanced technology nor the involvement of private companies can shield the United States or the Israeli regime from accountability for flagrant violations of their obligations under international law," Darzi told the council meeting. "Those responsible for the commission of atrocious crimes against Iranian people, including deliberate attacks against civilians and civilian objects, must face individual criminal accountability," he added. In March 2026 , the Commander of U.S. Central Command Adm. Brad Cooper confirmed American forces had used a "variety of advanced AI tools" in order to "cut through the noise and make smarter decisions faster than the enemy can react." While the Pentagon has not said exactly how AI tools are being deployed, CBS News spoke in March with several experts with knowledge of military operations who described the likely scenarios. "The military is now processing roughly a thousand potential targets a day and striking the majority of them, with turnaround time for the next strike potentially under four hours," said retired Navy Admiral Mark Montgomery, senior director of the Foundation for Defense of Democracy's Center on Cyber and Technology Innovation. "A human is still in the loop, but AI is doing the work that used to take days of analysis — and doing it at a scale no previous campaign has matched."

national.title: China investigates Politburo member and Shanghai party chief Chen Jining
national.summary: The Politburo member is the latest senior official targeted in President Xi Jinping's long-running anti-corruption campaign, which has shown no signs of letting up in scope or depth.
national.body:
FILE - Chen Jining, Communist Party Secretary for Shanghai attends a deliberation on the government work report, on the sideline of the National People's Congress at the Beijing Hotel, March 6, 2025. Ng Han Guan/AP hide caption

BANGKOK — Chinese Communist Party authorities are investigating Shanghai party secretary Chen Jining for suspected violations of party discipline, China's anti-corruption watchdog said Tuesday.

The Politburo member is the latest senior official targeted in President Xi Jinping's long-running anti-corruption campaign, which has shown no signs of letting up in scope or depth.

Chen is under investigation by the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection. The brief announcement by China's Central Commission for Discipline Inspection provided no further details.

A statement released by the Shanghai city government said the Standing Committee of the Shanghai Committee of the CCP "expressed firm support" for the decision to investigate Chen.

The decision sent "a clear and powerful signal that the fight against corruption would continue without pause or retreat," but with "a firm determination to win," the statement said.

The investigation follows sweeping purges under Xi, who has emphasized greater party discipline. The Chinese leader has pursued an anti-corruption campaign for more than a decade, carrying out purges on a scale not seen since Mao Zedong's rule.

"The takedown again shows that Xi Jinping's anti-corruption campaign has no limits," Mingda Qiu, a senior analyst at Eurasia Group, said in an emailed statement. "This is the fourth Politburo member to fall, and the fourth sitting member brought down in the current cycle. The pattern is unprecedented."

national.title: Small plane crash off Mississippi kills 6, including 2 children
national.summary: Six people, including two children, have been found dead after a plane crashed off the coast of Mississippi, according to the Coast Guard.
national.body: Six people, including two children, have been found dead after a plane crashed off the coast of Mississippi on Tuesday, according to the Coast Guard. Divers found their bodies in the fuselage of the aircraft after the Cessna 210 went down in the Gulf of Mexico between Pascagoula, Mississippi, and Horn Island, which is part of the Gulf Islands National Seashore, according to officials. There were four adults and two boys, ages 8 and 10, on board, said Coast Guard spokesperson Juan Ros.The air traffic control regional tower in Mobile, Alabama reported at about 3:45 p.m. that it had lost contact with the aircraft, the Coast Guard said. The Federal Aviation Administration said the plane was descending at 10,000 feet per minute when contact was lost, CBS Biloxi, Miss. affiliate WLOX-TV reported, citing the Coast Guard. Responders spent hours searching for the group and initially only found three life jackets, a life raft and the plane's cabin floating on the water, according to Ros.The Cessna was en route from New Orleans to Fort Myers, Florida, according to the flight tracking website FlightAware. Cmdr. Trevor Blount, the Coast Guard Sector Mobile Search and Rescue Mission Coordinator, called the situation heartbreaking. "While this is not the outcome any of us had hoped for, we are grateful for the strong interagency coordination that enabled us to swiftly locate those aboard the aircraft and provide closure to their families," he said in a statement. The FAA and National Transportation Safety Board will investigate the crash, with the NTSB taking the lead. Earlier this month, a Learjet 60 business jet nosedived into the ground in south Florida, killing all nine people on board. The terrifying crash was captured on video recorded by people inside their cars.

national.title: Zimbabwe issues arrest warrant for Robert Mugabe's son over missed court date
national.summary: The son of Zimbabwe's late former President Robert Mugabe has faced multiple legal troubles in the recent past.
national.body:
A Zimbabwean court has issued an arrest warrant for Bellarmine Chatunga Mugabe, the youngest son of the country's late former president Robert Mugabe, after he failed to appear in court.

Mugabe was arrested earlier this month alongside four others over assault allegations on a police officer during an investigation into the suspected smuggling of luxury vehicles.

The group subsequently faced charges of robbery and malicious damage to property. They have yet to enter pleas.

They were granted bail on 6 November and were due back in court on Tuesday. However, Mugabe failed to attend. His co-accused, an aide and three security guards appeared and were remanded until 10 December.

Prosecutors allege that Mugabe and the others assaulted an investigating officer using their hands and broomsticks.

The officer's phone was allegedly taken and smashed on the ground, while one of the accused is said to have seized the officer's loaded pistol.

Bellarmine Chatunga is the youngest son of Robert Mugabe and his second wife, Grace Mugabe.

Robert Mugabe ruled Zimbabwe for 37 years before being forced from power in 2017, aged 93, following a military intervention. He died in 2019.

national.title: Africa Cup title given back to Senegal after sports court rules against Morocco
national.summary: Senegal won the Africa Cup on the field in Morocco in January and then lost it in a legal case in March because its players walked off the field in protest in second-half stoppage time.
national.body:
FILE - Senegal's Sadio Mane holds the trophy aloft as he celebrates with teammates after winning the Africa Cup of Nations final soccer match between Senegal and Morocco in Rabat, Morocco, Sunday, Jan. 18, 2026. Youssef Loulidi/AP hide caption

More than 10 months on from a chaotic, controversial final, Senegal is Africa's soccer champion once again.

Senegal won back the Africa Cup of Nations title in a legal fight on Tuesday after the Court of Arbitration for Sport overturned an earlier ruling which handed the trophy to Morocco.

Senegal won the Africa Cup on the field in Morocco in January and then lost it in a legal case in March because its players walked off the field in protest in second-half stoppage time.

CAS has now rejected that earlier ruling, based on referee Jean-Jacques Ndala's decision to let the game resume after the protest.

"The Court of Arbitration for Sport has delivered justice to sport," Senegalese soccer federation president Abdoulaye Fall said in a statement.

The legal battle may not be over yet after Morocco announced plans to appeal, likely to Switzerland's supreme court, in a challenge to the integrity of a senior CAS judge.

Tournament regulations said a team which refuses to play should be considered to have lost the game, but CAS said those rules were meant only for cases "when a team's conduct leads the referee to call off the game permanently."

national.title: Kilmar Ábrego García leaves US for Spain, ending Trump deportation battle
national.summary: Ábrego García's deportation to El Salvador and return to the US became a flashpoint in the debate over President Donald Trump's immigration agenda.
national.body:
Kilmar Ábrego García, whose deportation last year to El Salvador sparked a bitter deportation battle, has left the US for Spain.

After the government admitted it had wrongfully sent Ábrego García to his home country, he was returned to the US to face human trafficking charges, which were later dropped. The administration then continued its attempts to send him to other countries, including Uganda and Ghana.

His deportation and return became a flashpoint in the debate over President Donald Trump's immigration agenda.

Ábrego García, who is married to a US citizen and lived in Maryland, came to the US illegally from El Salvador as a teenager.

Senator Chris Van Hollen, a Democrat from Maryland, visited Ábrego García while he was in the notorious Cecot prison in El Salvador in 2025 and advocated for his release.

"A year and a half ago, the Trump Administration wanted to leave Kilmar Ábrego García to rot in a Salvadoran gulag," Van Hollen said in a statement on Tuesday. "Today, Kilmar is travelling to a country of his choice, a free man - unharmed and with dignity."

In a statement, Ábrego García's lawyer said his departure was "temporary" as he had "many options to return to the United States".

"We don't expect that to happen under this administration, which we know will never give him a fair shake, but we expect that the next administration will prioritize reunifying this family and bringing him back to Maryland," the statement said.

national.title: Four years after huge asteroid crash, a spacecraft has now returned to assess the damage
national.summary: The mission is studying an asteroid deliberately knocked off course by a colliding spacecraft.
national.body:
A spacecraft has arrived at an asteroid to investigate the damage caused by an unprecedented cosmic crash.

It what may sound like the plot of a disaster movie, Nasa's Dart spacecraft deliberately smashed into the space rock in 2022 to knock it off course.

The Nasa craft was obliterated on impact. Four years on, a European Space Agency (ESA) mission, called Hera, is scouring the scene to fully assess the aftermath of the collision - with the first images set to be released later on Wednesday.

The asteroid poses no threat, instead this was the first ever test of our planetary defences to see what action we could take if a space rock was heading for our planet.

"Hera is a sort of Inspector Columbo going back to the crash scene to investigate what is the outcome of this impact," said Patrick Michel, principal investigator of ESA's Hera mission.

The crash test focussed on a pair of asteroids: a larger one called Didymos - about 730m (2,400ft) wide - which is orbited by a smaller rock called Dimorphos, about 150m (490ft) wide.

The Dart spacecraft targeted Dimorphos, hurtling into the rock at 22,000km per hour (14,000mph). Images beamed back showed the asteroid's rocky surface coming ever closer until the feed cut out on impact.

It was such a big smash-up that the trail of debris, measuring about 10,000km long (6,200 miles), was spotted by telescopes on Earth and in space.

national.summary: The wife of Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk, who is currently aboard the International Space Station, gave birth to the couple's third child, Canadian officials announced.
national.body: The wife of a Canadian astronaut who is currently aboard the International Space Station gave birth Tuesday to the couple's third child, Canadian officials announced. Heather Kutryk, the wife of astronaut Joshua Kutryk, gave birth to a girl, the Canadian Space Agency said in a news release. "Heather and baby are both doing well," the agency said, adding that Joshua Kutryk was able to share in the experience from the space station. "Joshua is currently living out a childhood dream aboard the International Space Station," the couple said in a statement. "Even with the distance between us, we feel incredibly connected as we welcome our new little star into our lives."The couple's two other children are ages 7 and 5. Joshua Kutryk traveled to the space station on Oct. 1 from Florida aboard a SpaceX Crew Dragon capsule as part of Crew 13, accompanied by two NASA astronauts and a Russian cosmonaut.In an interview just prior to his departure, he told CBS News that it would be tough to miss the birth, but that he would "try to take the positive things out of it." "Physically, of course, I won't be here, but as hard as that will be, it also lends itself to what I hope will be a very unique and enriching life experience that we'll look on fondly," Joshua Kutryk said. In the history of space travel, Joshua Kutryk is just the fourth astronaut to miss the birth of a child. A former military test pilot, this was Kutryk's first spaceflight. He is the 17th Canadian to fly in space. "We have an enormous support network, and we feel just happy and joyful to be doing this," he said in that interview. "This is a hard job. There's a lot of good things about it, there's some bad things. One of those bad things is that it's very unpredictable, and you can't predict when things like launches are going to happen."Crew 13 does not yet have a confirmed date for its return to Earth. Kutryk told CBS News: "We think it's exceptionally important, and I hope that my new child looks at it as such, as making some sacrifice, taking some risk, but doing so in the name of public service and the name, in my case, for Canada."

national.title: Huawei found guilty of stealing US trade secrets but acquitted of racketeering
national.summary: The verdict follows a months-long trial in New York.
national.body:
Huawei has been found guilty of conspiracy to steal trade secrets and bank fraud, but not guilty of the more serious overarching racketeering charge in a landmark case in the US.

In a two-month trial, prosecutors accused the Chinese technology and telecommunications giant of lying, cheating and stealing to gain any competitive advantage.

Huawei's defence team argued that prosecutors had decided Huawei was a criminal organisation and built its case from there, but the firm's success was due to its own innovation.

Huawei said , external the racketeering acquittal "confirms that these allegations lack factual basis", adding that it would "take all necessary legal actions to defend our rights and interests".

Jurors in a Brooklyn court found Huawei guilty of 10 out of 12 counts, which included conspiracy to violate US sanctions.

However, the jury declined to convict Huawei of the racketeering conspiracy charge, which required members to find the firm acted like a criminal enterprise.

Federal prosecutors first announced the charges against Huawei in 2019, after the dramatic arrest in late 2018 of senior executive Meng Wanzhou in Canada.

Meng, also known as Cathy Meng, was held for three years in Canada before she was released to return to China through a deal with US prosecutors.

national.title: She spent decades as an FBI agent and this is the case she could not let go
national.summary: Jane Collins had all but given up on seeing Michael Donovan and Richard Moore face justice. Then they were charged with stealing from a mass-shooter’s brother.
national.body:
Jane Collins had spent 30 years as an FBI agent, but there was one case that haunted her long after retirement.

Michael Donovan was a fraudster, former minister and multimillionaire she had pursued for years, and even in her retirement she could not escape him.

He was regularly featured in the news and on the radio, appearing as a spokesperson for a number of causes, from migrant rights to anti-racism and justice reform.

He and his husband, Richard Moore, lived about an hour's drive from her, in Augusta County, Virginia, on the edge of the Appalachian Mountains.

Together they owned a business, Libre by Nexus, which had made more than $200m (£152m) from migrants seeking release from US immigrant detention centres - but it was a scam, government regulators said.

They were fined $811m for conning detained migrants, but the scams didn't stop

She had investigated Nexus from 2016 until her retirement from the FBI in 2021. But the only federal criminal charges either faced - after almost six years of her investigation - was a tax charge against Moore.

So when Collins left the bureau, there were still a few strands left of her investigation that she could not let go - like the case of Zach Cruz, the brother of the man who killed 17 people in Parkland, Florida.

national.title: 'This could be apocalyptic' - Iowans hunker down for controlled blast of explosives stockpile
national.summary: Some residents tell the BBC that Wednesday's detonation could be life-changing, while others just want it to be over.
national.body:
Iowans are hunkering down as the US Army plans to blow up five tonnes of degraded explosives on Wednesday, with some fearing the controlled blast could be disastrous, even as others just want it over and done with.

The Army has argued a controlled detonation of 68 barrels of lead azide, a highly volatile compound used as a detonator, is necessary to protect the public from an unplanned explosion - something it said would become more likely as temperatures are due to fall in the coming days.

The detonation at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in the city of Middletown is to go ahead after an appeals court overturned an earlier decision to stop the blast over concerns about the potential health and environmental hazards of lead exposure.

Officials have announced a five-mile (8km) optional evacuation zone and a 20-mile shelter-in-place advisory, with potential airborne lead dust reaching up to 100 miles, depending on weather and wind.

Those who have chosen to stay have been told to remain indoors around the blast time and to expect "temporary noise, ground vibrations, and a dust plume that will contain some lead".

Many people in the area are from families who have been there for generations – working in farming, manufacturing or at the ammunition plant itself.

Margo Sprenger, 71, a farmer and landowner in Donnelson, about 20 miles south-west of the factory, said her land was in the direct path of the projected plume and that "it's going to change my life forever".

"Our grandparents started on these farms, and now we don't even know if they can produce food that we can trust," she said.

national.title: Lies, a disguise and surfboard bags: How a jealous Sydney policeman tried to cover up double murder
national.summary: Beau Lamarre was on Wednesday found guilty of murdering his ex Jesse Baird, and Baird's new partner Luke Davies.
national.body:
It was just after 09:00 on a warm February morning when CCTV picked up a man dressed as an UberEats rider hovering on a sidewalk in one of Sydney's wealthiest neighbourhoods.

He dawdled for around 20 minutes, "steeling himself for what he was about to do" prosecutors say, before disappearing out of sight. Minutes later another CCTV camera captured the sound of gunshots ringing out.

Former police officer Beau Lamarre, 31, was on Wednesday found guilty of murdering his former partner Jesse Baird, a TV presenter, and Luke Davies, Baird's new partner, with his work-issued gun.

In February 2024, the bloodied belongings of Baird and Davies were found in a skip in the suburb of Cronulla, sparking a frantic search for the couple. It culminated in the discovery of their bodies on a rural property, partially buried beneath sticks and debris.

During a two-month trial filled with at-times extraordinary testimony and a wealth of CCTV evidence, the court heard Lamarre had planned his crime over months.

Jurors watched CCTV of the then police officer purchasing a surfboard bag in which to put Baird's body, after casually sizing it up against a friend in the shop, and heard from a stream of former friends and colleagues who testified that Lamarre asked them for advice about everything from mobile phone signals to where he could buy a gun.

One recounted the chilling moment Lamarre told her that if he were ever to murder someone, he would leave their belongings in a dumpster and hide the body in bushland where they would never be found.

"What would you do if I told you I killed somebody? Would you help me hide the body?" he asked, according to her testimony.

national.title: Trump's rescue of Nvidia's Huang brings political risks
national.summary: The US president's intercession to reinstate CEO Jensen Huang has inextricably linked their fates.
national.body:
After the AI chipmaker Nvidia announced it was bringing back embattled former head Jensen Huang and the company's stock shot up like a bullet, President Donald Trump took a very public victory lap.

"I made the deal," he said during a lengthy phone interview with cable business news channel CNBC.

Trump followed that with an AI-generated image posted to his social media platform that riffed on the famous photograph taken moments after the 2024 attempt on his life in Pennsylvania. But instead of Trump in the image, Huang was the one surrounded by Secret Service guards. It depicted him in front of an Nvidia banner - with a raised fist clenching a red bra.

The post was classic Trump – potentially offensive, yet still a bit opaque.

Was Trump suggesting Huang survived a scandal – one that includes allegations of recklessly jeopardising US national security by consorting with a suspected Chinese spy – the way he had survived an assassin's bullet?

Was the bra a celebration Huang's reported extramarital affairs? By replacing the US flag with an Nvidia standard, was he claiming that America and one of its largest, most powerful companies are one and the same?

At the very least, the image underscores how inextricably linked Huang and Trump now are, with the fate of the former hinging on the successes and failures of the latter.

And with that comes significant risks for the American president and for Republicans, including Vice-President JD Vance, who played a key part in his efforts to rescue Huang.

national.summary: India's food inflation is broadening, squeezing household budgets.
national.body:
India correspondent Published 9 hours ago India's inflation is rising again. And the biggest worry is what's happening to food prices.

The latest government data , external shows retail inflation climbed to 6.09% in October, up from 5.54% in September.

But look more closely at food inflation. It has surged to 8.94%.

The squeeze was sharper in rural India, where food inflation was 9.09%, compared with 8.68% in urban areas.

In other words, food prices are rising considerably faster than the overall rate of inflation.

Food inflation this year has been driven by a combination of weather disruptions, supply shortages and rising input costs, say economists.

With nearly 60% of its farmland dependent on rainfall , external , India remains acutely vulnerable to the vagaries of the monsoon. This year, the southwest monsoon was 13% below normal and unevenly distributed, while intensifying El Niño conditions have heightened risks to farm production.

A survey by polling agency LocalCircles found that six in 10 consumers say household essentials cost them over 20% more each month than a year ago, prompting calls for government intervention.

national.title: Shot in the face at 15: The lives shattered by Cameroon's decade of conflict

national.body:
She remembers the date vividly - 7 April 2018. She was ill and confined to her bed.

Armed men stormed her family's compound in Cameroon's Southwest region, one of the country's two English-speaking areas at the centre of a separatist conflict.

Median, now 23, says she was fast asleep when her brother woke her, panicked by the approach of a group of armed men who were shooting indiscriminately.

He escaped through a window. But for Median, fleeing was not so easy.

"Since I was sick, I had no strength to jump through the window with him, so I had to pass through the door," she tells the BBC.

She says she came face to face with two of the attackers in the backyard, who opened fire at her.

They first shot her in the thigh before firing several more rounds, which severely damaged her face.

"I kept pleading with them not to kill me, that I wasn't feeling well. However, I found myself on the floor," she recalls.

national.title: Clashing political visions reflect a divided Spain ahead of election
national.summary: Sunday’s election could see a far-right party enter the Spanish government for first time.
national.body:
Speaking in a wrestling ring on the island of Tenerife as he campaigned ahead of Sunday's general election, Spain's Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez cautioned those listening about the spread of right-wing governments.

"What good has President [Donald] Trump done the United States and, by extension, the world - was he a change or a step backwards?" he asked supporters, before invoking the administrations of Brazil's former leader, Jair Bolsonaro, and Argentinian President Javier Milei.

"If we don't want that for the world, why would we want it for our own country?" said Sánchez.

He issued his warning as Spain's conservative People's Party (PP) leads most of the polls and appears poised to form a governing coalition with the hard-right Vox. The election comes amid a deeply polarised political atmosphere in which both left and right have warned about their opponents' ability to undermine democracy.

In a Europe dominated by right-leaning governments, Sánchez has gained a reputation as the continent's most outspoken and uncompromising left-wing prime minister.

His strident rhetoric defending feminism, immigration and green energy, along with his condemnation of Israel's military action in Gaza and verbal clashes with Trump, has fostered this image.

Having overseen consistent economic growth in recent years, his stock is high among the international left.

Yet in Spain, Sánchez has become a hate figure for the right, who see him as an autocrat with little regard for the separation of state powers, obsessed with clinging on to power and surrounded by a corrupt cabal.

national.body: Officials are searching for a man who went overboard during a cruise vacation on board Royal Caribbean's Allure of the Seas, according to Bahamian officials.The Allure of the Seas is on an eight-day Thanksgiving cruise in the Caribbean that departed from Miami on Sunday. The cruise line called out a passenger's name over the ship's loudspeaker system for several hours before determining that the man had gone overboard, according to passengers on board the cruise ship. The ship then turned around to look for him, the passengers said. The ship's captain announced Monday that the crew had "received a report of a missing guest" earlier in the day before determining "that the guest had unfortunately gone overboard," according to two recordings of a captain's announcement obtained by CBS News.Christian Bunse, a passenger aboard the ship, told CBS Miami, "People got quiet when they heard it, because they heard his name again."Royal Caribbean told CBS News that it "immediately launched a search and rescue effort" to find the man and are working with authorities.The Coast Guard said the Allure of the Seas alerted it and the Royal Bahamian Defense Force of a man overboard at around 11:30 p.m. on Monday. The Coast Guard said the man was reported to have gone overboard off the coast of San Salvador Island, Bahamas. The Royal Bahamian Defense Force is leading search efforts for the man, aided by the Coast Guard. "We are coordinating with the cruise and will have a vessel on scene," said a spokesperson for the Royal Bahamas Defence Force. Royal Caribbean said its care team is providing "support and assistance to the guest's loved ones." A woman fell from her balcony on the Allure of the Seas on a Taylor Swift-themed cruise in October 2024. Dulcie White's family alleged in a lawsuit that Royal Caribbean's unlimited drink package encouraged overconsumption, and that crew members ignored clear warning signs before the fatal fall. Her body was never recovered. The case remains ongoing.

national.title: Russia's own figures show it has lost almost 500,000 people in Ukraine war
national.summary: Leaked data reveal how the full-scale invasion of Ukraine has fundamentally changed mortality patterns in Russia.
national.body:
At least 490,334 Russian soldiers have died since the start of the war in Ukraine in 2022, according to Russian government statistics analysed by the BBC.

The leaked Rosstat data reveal how the full-scale invasion of Ukraine has fundamentally changed mortality patterns in Russia, and show the high cost paid in human life in a war that Vladimir Putin had assumed would last only days but is now almost five years old.

BBC Russian has had access to more than 11 million death records from 2021 to September 2026, after a hack by Belarusian group Cyber Partisans BY and Ukraine's Silent Crow.

Russia's statistics agency admitted to a cyber-attack, but denied any protected information had been leaked.

Together with independent Russian outlet Mediazona, BBC Russian has compared the Rosstat data with its own list of confirmed military deaths, pulled from open sources since the start of the invasion, and it has found matches for 90% of the records.

Military experts estimate that the BBC's list of 290,012 deaths, gleaned from official reports, social media, new memorials and graves, may account for 45-55% of the true death toll, which would range from 527,295 to 644,471.

The records show that 65% of 18 to 24 year-olds in Russia who lost their lives in 2025 died in the war. For those aged 25-34 the number was 59%. Only among 45 to 54 year-olds does cardiovascular disease claim more Russian lives than the conflict.

The data also reveal the extent of losses in specific areas of Ukraine. Some 20,000 Russian soldiers died fighting for control of 10 Ukrainian villages whose combined pre-war population was 12,000.

national.title: My family died in Ukraine. My mum blamed Zelensky's troops - the truth is complicated
national.summary: BBC journalist Anastasiya Gribanova investigates who killed her father and grandparents in the war.
national.body:
I am sitting on my balcony in Kyiv looking at a photo of a garden in the village I grew up in, in eastern Ukraine. The plot is overgrown with thick grass, and two wooden stakes are planted in the ground. Despite the warm sunshine, I find myself shivering.

The woman who sent me the photo says the stakes mark the graves of my grandparents, killed as the Ukrainian-Russian front line reached our little community. Not far away, in another garden in the village, the body of my father, Serezha, is buried in a greenhouse.

I cover the Russia-Ukraine war for the BBC World Service, but found myself in the middle of that story in February last year when my mother sent me a devastating text message.

"Granny, grandad and Serezha are gone. Now there is no-one left," it said.

Because not only had I lost three beloved family members, my mother blamed Ukraine for their deaths - the country where I was born and have lived for most of my life.

Mum was born in Siberia. From the moment Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, she had supported Russia in the conflict.

Backing Moscow is not that unusual in the Donbas region - the predominantly Russian-speaking part of eastern Ukraine where my village Dachne is located.

After pro-Russian forces captured large parts of the Donbas in 2014, many of those who stayed supported Moscow over Kyiv, a stance cemented by exposure to Russian state TV.

local.summary: In the basement of the College of Art and Design, Professor Ahasan Habib picks up a flat, flexible, web-like printout that illustrates one step of many toward a dream to bio-print skin grafts, prosthetics and, one day, organs.
local.body:
Listen • 1:38 Rochester Institute of Technology researchers are working to create something like skin from scratch.

In the basement of the College of Art and Design, Professor Ahasan Habib picks up a flat, flexible, web-like printout that had been sitting in a drawer. It illustrates one step of many toward a dream to biologically print skin grafts, prosthetics and, one day, organs using a 3D printer.

"As an engineer, our goal is to make the technology that, like really, doctor, biomedical engineer, or biomedical professionals can use it for their purpose," Habib said.

Habib's vision is to use a type of material that is mostly comprised of water called hydrogel, infuse it with someone's stem cells, and then 3D print that concoction into tissue that would then become part of that person's body, with minimal risk of rejection — theoretically.

It's a vision shared by many in the interdisciplinary field of biotechnology. NASA astronauts have performed tests in microgravity in recent years, and researchers at the University of Miami’s Miller School of Medicine have an entire facility dedicated to 3D bioprinting.

In practice, there are logistical problems to solve before that could become reality. Such as: What exactly is the right combination of material to work with to account for the complexities of the human body?

"There's all sorts of parameters like even outside of like the very physical, like does it print well?" said Schuyler Mann, a dual-degree student in the engineering department. "Does it resist UV light? Can it support bacteria, if that's important for the application? How well can it sustain itself on its own?"

Mann is months away from graduation, and he works with Habib on bioprinting research for his capstone project.

local.title: Native Made Market brings Indigenous artisans, fashion and culture to downtown Rochester
local.summary: The fifth annual event will take over the Central Library downtown this weekend on Small Business Saturday, blending holiday shopping with cultural preservation.
local.body:
Rochester’s fifth annual Native Made Market will take over the Central Library downtown this weekend on Small Business Saturday, blending holiday shopping with cultural preservation.

The free gathering will feature Indigenous artisans, designers and educators from across Rochester, along with traditional dance, storytelling and fashion shows representing all six Haudenosaunee nations.

For Angelina Hilton, organizing Rochester’s Native Made Market is personal.

She’s an enrolled member of the Sac and Fox Nation, and she said fewer than 500 members remain in the Kansas-based tribe — a reality that adds urgency to bringing Native American culture into the wider community.

"It's important to preserve the fact that we were here and are still here, and are going to be here, because we're here to steward for at least the next seven generations," she said.

Hilton launched the market in 2022 inside her family’s cafe to counter what she saw as a lack of visibility for local Native people. Bringing a gathering to the Central Library carries its own significance, she said.

"We're telling our own stories in a place that shares stories with community, which hasn't historically, authentically represented Indigenous people and voices," Hilton said.

The market will be held from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. Saturday at Rochester’s Central Library on South Avenue. Admission is free.

local.body:
For hunting and fishing families across Western New York, Thanksgiving is about much more than turkey, stuffing and pumpkin pie. It’s a celebration of family, tradition, the outdoors, and the wonderful harvest that comes from the woods, waters and farms we are fortunate to call home.

Of course, a traditional Thanksgiving dinner wouldn’t be complete without the familiar favorites: a golden turkey, mashed potatoes and gravy, homemade stuffing, cranberry relish, squash, Brussels sprouts and a collection of pies that somehow always find room on an already crowded table. In many outdoor households, there’s also room for something a little more wild.

Venison, bear, pheasant, duck, wild turkey, rabbit and locally caught fish can all find their way onto our local holiday menu. These dishes bring something special to the celebration: a connection to the outdoors, memories of successful hunts and fishing trips, and the satisfaction of sharing food harvested by family and friends.

A few years ago, I had the pleasure of meeting Moira Tidball of Seneca County, a Cornell Cooperative Extension nutrition educator and the founder of the Wild Harvest Table. Launched in January 2009, the website celebrates the culinary bounty of wild game and fish throughout New York’s Finger Lakes region. It offers tested recipes, nutritional information and practical preparation techniques that make cooking wild harvests approachable and enjoyable.

Moira’s partner, Dr. Keith G. Tidball of Cornell University’s Department of Natural Resources and Environment, helped bring the project to life, recognizing its potential to explore the connections between hunting, fishing, food and community. Along with Dr. Paul Curtis of DNRE, the team secured USDA funding for research titled Leveraging the Locavore Movement: Exploring Family and Community Food Decision-making. The project examined how locally harvested foods influence the ways families procure, prepare and enjoy their meals. The effort also helped bring nutritional information for several wild species into USDA FoodData Central.

The result is a terrific resource for anyone looking to bring a little more wild harvest to the dinner table. From venison and bear to squirrel, grouse, pheasant, waterfowl, wild turkey, walleye, trout and bass, there’s plenty of inspiration to be found at www.wildharvesttable.com. I’ve tried the recipes myself, and they’re delicious without requiring a culinary degree or an entire afternoon of kitchen negotiations.

local.title: Trustees seek direct Dunkirk water link
local.summary: Fredonia’s incessant water supply debate saw another bend in its stream Monday. Two trustees are suggesting a halt on plans to connect with the North County Water District through the town of Pomfret’s infrastructure. Trustees Tim Mulholland and LeeAnn Lazarony want Fredonia to instead revisit a pla
local.body:
Fredonia's incessant water supply debate saw another bend in its stream Monday. Two trustees are suggesting a halt on plans to connect with the North County Water District through the town of Pomfret's infrastructure.

Trustees Tim Mulholland and LeeAnn Lazarony want Fredonia to instead revisit a plan for connecting directly with the city of Dunkirk.

"This was actually something that was looked at," Mulholland noted at a Board of Trustees meeting. He did most of the talking about the proposal; Lazarony was attending remotely and had occasional microphone issues.

Indeed, a previous edition of Fredonia's Board of Trustees approved a plan to connect directly with Dunkirk in December 2023. However, a group of village residents successfully sued to halt that plan. No one mentioned that lawsuit at Tuesday's meeting.

Fredonia later pivoted to its current plan to connect with the NCWD through Pomfret -- though it recently suspended engineering on the project due to funding issues. Dunkirk's water plant also supplies the NCWD in addition to the city's own direct customers.

"The fact that the interconnection worked really triggered this thought process again for us," Mulholland said. The village acquired more than 900,000 gallons from Dunkirk, through an existing line that connects with a pump station on Vineyard Drive, in October during boil water and conservation orders. However, that line does not have sufficient capacity to supply all of Fredonia's water needs.

Mulholland stated NCWD "engineers have identified several steps in their preliminary plans making (the current connection plan) a complicated proposal." He noted that pressure reducing valves, new mains and a new storage tank would be required.

That would drive the project costs over $21.5 million, he said. But estimated costs of connecting directly with Dunkirk in 2023 were only around $5 million, he said.

local.summary: Measles cases in Chautauqua County have hit double digits. It was announced at the Chautauqua County Board of Health meeting Thursday that there have been 10 cases of measles reported in the county. According to the state’s measles dashboard website, that number had not increased as of Tuesday morni
local.body:
It was announced at the Chautauqua County Board of Health meeting Thursday that there have been 10 cases of measles reported in the county. According to the state's measles dashboard website, that number had not increased as of Tuesday morning.

Lacey Wilson, Chautauqua County public health director, said due to privacy laws, the state won't report the outbreak by zip codes.

"There's so few numbers, they could easily be identifiable," she said.

Wilson declined to say if any of those individuals have been hospitalized. She did add that there have been no deaths due to measles in Chautauqua County as of the time of the interview.

For those who suspect they may have measles, Wilson asked people to call their doctor first instead of going directly to the emergency room.

"What we're concerned about is exposure to other people, so call a health care provider and seek their guidance as to what your next steps should be," she said.

On Sept. 2 health officials announced the first case of measles of measles in Chautauqua County in more than 30 years.

For neighboring New York counties, Erie County has two cases, while Cattaraugus County has five confirmed cases.

local.title: Shop local on Small Business Saturday
local.summary: The holiday shopping season has begun, and please do not overlook your local small businesses! This year, Small Business Saturday will take place on Nov. 28, the Saturday after Thanksgiving. This is the perfect opportunity to support your local community. Small businesses are the engines that fuel o
local.body:
The holiday shopping season has begun, and please do not overlook your local small businesses! This year, Small Business Saturday will take place on Nov. 28, the Saturday after Thanksgiving.

This is the perfect opportunity to support your local community. Small businesses are the engines that fuel our neighborhoods, providing jobs, boosting our economy, and adding character, value, and spirit to Main Street.

As New York's assistant state director of the National Federation of Independent Business, I hear from owners who have put years of work and much of their savings into building a business. They know customers have choices. Earning their business takes good service, quality products and fair prices. For shoppers, that personal attention can make a difference.

Unfortunately, many storefronts across New York state are vacant due to unending challenges. From high inflation, rising utility costs, changing consumer habits, and other economic pressures, small businesses are struggling to stay afloat. However, there is a way to help! This Small Business Saturday, make it a point to use your dollars where it counts by shopping and dining at local, independently owned businesses.

You can also support local shops and restaurants on a busy schedule. Many small businesses let customers browse and buy online. Some provide delivery or curbside pickup. Visit their websites, check their social media pages or call to ask what's available.

And did you know that 67 cents of every dollar spent at a local small business is reinvested in the community?

Shopping locally at your mom-and-pop shops is an investment in our local tax base, governments, and schools, while also enriching our communities. But small businesses not only generate direct economic benefits; 90 percent of small businesses contribute to community and civic groups, including youth sports leagues, community events, charities, and school programs. Small businesses support us, and now it’s our turn to support them.

As we enter this busy time of year, it may be tempting to order online from large retail giants for convenience. However, let’s not forget our neighbors, friends, and family members who own small businesses. The 17th annual Small Business Saturday is on Nov. 28, reminding us to support our local Main Street businesses. This Saturday and throughout the entire holiday season, consider shopping small. New York’s small businesses need our support now more than ever!

local.summary: After more than 20 years working outside Dunkirk, Habitat for Humanity, in conjunction with the Land Bank, is working on its second Dunkirk house in the last two years. The first house, on Genet Street was completed late summer of 2025 and the new house on Hoyt Street is in the process of being side
local.body:
After more than 20 years working outside Dunkirk, Habitat for Humanity, in conjunction with the Land Bank, is working on its second Dunkirk house in the last two years. The first house, on Genet Street was completed late summer of 2025 and the new house on Hoyt Street is in the process of being sided.

Once the siding is complete the house will be closed up until after the holiday season when there will be a Habitat family selected for the house.

In July, thanks to Kevin Muldowney of Route 5 Warehouse and Business Park, Habitat for Humanity was allowed to build and store both the exterior and interior walls inside one of the rooms in his storage facility, located on Route 5, Dunkirk.

These walls then had to be moved to 432 Hoyt St., Dunkirk. Assisting in the move of the walls to the location of the new house were four employees from Excelco of Silver Creek, the firm that also supplied two flatbed trucks to make the move of over 40 sections of walls possible. In addition, there were two employees from Route 5 Warehouse who assisted in this muscle demanding endeavor. CAHFH is so very grateful for the able-bodied assistance of these businesses and their employees, along with our "regular" volunteers.

Grading and foundation work were completed by Beaver Brothers Construction, thus making the move possible on Aug. 11 to 12 when the trucks and the men helped us move and erect over 40 sections of walls at Hoyt Street. "Thanks to Mark Fortner and his crew, the trusses and roof were on the house a week later. Gugino Plumbing has worked to get water and sewer lines to the house as well as setting up the bathrooms and the air circulation system. John Castiglia, master electrician of BECC Electric, has overseen a crew of students from Job Corps who have been pulling wires to the box," Habitat for Humanity said in a news release.

As you can imagine, building a Habitat house needs and receives help from all kinds of businesses, but the backbone of the organization is the group of dedicated volunteers who show up week after week to provide a home for a family in need of simple, affordable housing. Many thanks to our unsung heroes.

"If you are looking for a chance to contribute to the work – – – come and join us!" Habitat for Humanity said. "We work at 432 Hoyt St. most Saturdays from 8:30 a.m. to 12:30 p.m., but interested new volunteers can call 716-863-4475 to make sure that work will take place on a specific Saturday. All volunteers ages 18 and over are welcome."

Author and scholar Michael Leroy Oberg brings the struggles and the resilience of the Onondaga Nation to life in his book, “The Central Fire of the Iroquois: A Five-Hundred-Year History of the Onondaga Nation.”

Oberg writes of the many threats and attacks on the Indigenous population. The story involves a rise, a fall, and a rise into the modern era, along with the hope of self-determination.

For those who feel like they don’t fully understand the story of the Onondaga Nation — or who were taught only caricatures — these lessons will be new and vital.

The 300,000-square-foot property will house DPW employees as well as equipment that keeps the city working, such as snow plows and garbage trucks. The move comes after the Ryan administration issued a declaration of emergency following a partial roof collapse on the second floor of the Broadway Barns in October. The barn roof if full of holes and has been crumbling for decades.On Tuesday Deputy Mayor Benjamin Swanekamp told 7 News he was "thankful and relieved" the council approved the new deal. "This truly is a huge, this is a gamechanger," Swanekamp said. "This is a generational change for the Department of Public Works."DPW workers have been operating out of the Broadway Barns since 1948, which was the last time the building had any major upgrades according to Swanekamp. "So now we get to move our hardworking men and women to a new modern and safe facility, so this is fantastic news and DPW's ready to hit the ground running," Swanekamp told me.The lease agreement for 231 Ship Canal Parkway lasts for 10 years at $2.5 million a year for the first three years. local.title: Gowanda community comes together to help local families ahead of the holidays
local.summary: Gowanda neighbors are coming together to help local families put food on the table this holiday season.
local.body: As families across Western New York prepare for the holidays, people in Gowanda are finding ways to make sure their neighbors have food on the table.The Gowanda Food Pantry recently received a delivery from FeedMore, helping replenish its shelves ahead of the busy holiday season. Local businesses and community members are also pitching in through food drives and other donation efforts.One of those efforts is happening at Gowanda Shop & Save, which is offering Gowanda Give Back Bags to give customers an opportunity to donate food to local families.Jessica Fort, whose family is involved with the store, says the community response has been encouraging."We had an overwhelming response last year, it went great. The community really does come together and help each other out," Fort said.A separate community food drive recently collected approximately 2,000 pounds of food for the pantry.While the donations make a significant difference, pantry officials say the need remains constant.Desiree Sanderson, director of the Gowanda Food Pantry, said the food collected through the recent drive is expected to last about two weeks.Sanderson said the pantry served 212 families for Thanksgiving and expects to serve just as many for Christmas.The pantry provides more than 63,000 meals each year to people in the Gowanda area, highlighting the continued demand for food assistance in the rural community.That need reflects a broader challenge across the country. Feeding America's 2026 Map the Meal Gap report found that more than eight in 10 counties with the highest estimated food insecurity rates are rural or located in the South.For volunteers like Michael Rice, the effort is about more than putting food on pantry shelves. It's about making sure people who may be struggling know their community is behind them."It's the driving force of the community. To assist those who are forgotten, those who seem to have no agency for themselves, so we can help build that, partner with them, so they can better their condition on a daily basis," Rice said.As Christmas approaches, pantry officials and community partners say continued donations and local support will remain important in helping families get through the holiday season.

local.title: New York bans AI chatbot toys
local.summary: The five-year ban applies to toys like talking stuffed animals, dolls or robots and comes amid safety concerns about some of the conversations children are having with those objects.
local.body:
New York Gov. Kathy Hochul signed a bill Tuesday that places a moratorium on AI chatbots in children’s toys.

The five-year ban applies to toys like talking stuffed animals, dolls or robots and comes amid safety concerns about some of the conversations children are having with those objects.

California recently took similar action , and Pennsylvania is considering its own moratorium .

New York’s prohibition takes effect in 90 days, so Hochul warned parents about the potential risk of purchasing toys with chatbots for holiday gifts in the meantime.

She also indicated more AI safety proposals are coming as part of her State of the State address early next year.

“We'll set clear safety standards and put independent experts inside these companies to make sure that they're following the rules, and that we'll insist that humans remain in control, and with plans to contain the danger if something does go wrong,” Hochul said.

Toy manufacturing, sellers or operators of AI companions face $15,000 per day per violation of the ban, which would be enforced by the Attorney General.

The ban follows other legislation aimed at AI safety, including age verification and warnings labels on social media sites for users under 18. Those laws have faced legal challenges by groups representing big tech firms.

local.title: Monroe County proposal aims to prevent people from becoming homeless
local.summary: Project Home would provide some public assistance recipients with larger housing allowances to prevent them from becoming homeless.
local.body:
Monroe County wants to nearly double the amount of public assistance money it provides individuals and families facing homelessness. But it needs state approval to do so.

The county wants to shift $2.8 million in public assistance funds to the effort, which officials are calling Project Home. The program provides larger housing allowances — up to 60% of fair market rent — to public assistance recipients most at risk of becoming homeless It would assist up to 600 households.

"That additional support will be the difference between a family falling behind on rent, (or) staying current," County Executive Adam Bello said. "It could mean the parents keeping their children in the same home, in a stable home, in the same school, surrounded by the same friends and support systems."

The county also would use the money to help people who have been staying in shelters for a long time be able to transition to a permanent residence.

Project Home is Monroe County's way of addressing what has been a long-term, state-level problem with deficient public assistance. The state sets the schedule for public assistance grants, but it hasn't boosted the amounts in decades even though housing costs have greatly increased.

Currently, a family of four receiving public assistance gets $374 to cover rent. The federally-calculated market rate for an efficiency apartment in Monroe County is roughly $1,000.

"The result has been a system that pays to keep people in shelters instead of supporting stable permanent housing," Bello said. "We cannot expect families to find housing stability when the support designed to help them doesn't help."

During a news conference Tuesday, several Democratic legislators and community leaders spoke in favor of the proposal. Among then was Aqua Porter, executive of the Rochester-Monroe County Anti-Poverty Initiative.

Phil Collins has called time on touring, but he’s not against a collaboration with blink-182’s Travis Barker .

That was one of the unlikely outcomes of the Rock And Roll Hall of Fame induction ceremony last weekend, at which Barker had the honors of saluting fellow drummer Collins.

Barker stopped by ABC’s Jimmy Kimmel Live on Tuesday night (Nov. 24), for a chat about his growing tapestry of tattoos (he does get approval from his wife, Kourtney Kardashian, if they’re above his shoulders), his documentary, and the career highlight that was his moment at the podium, with Collins by his side — thanks to a rare mistimed moment from the veteran British rocker. “I was a huge Phil Collins fan. My mom introduced me to him when I was really young. Four, five, six years old,” Barker tells Kimmel. The youngster studied Collins’ work behind the kit, listened to his tunes until the grooves in the records wore out. entertainment.title: ‘Star Trek’ star Jonathan Frakes says bladder cancer discovery followed one strange bathroom symptom
entertainment.summary: "My pee was pink," Jonathan Frakes shared during an episode of his podcast "Dropping Names with Brent and Jonny,"
entertainment.body:
For “Star Trek: The Next Generation” star Jonathan Frakes, a life-altering health scare began not with physical pain, but with a strange sighting during a regular trip to Phoenix.

“My pee was pink,” Frakes shared during an episode of his podcast, “Dropping Names with Brent and Jonny,” alongside his co-star Brent Spiner and urologic surgeon Dr. Ram Narayanan. “I was unnerved.”

Searching for an easy explanation, Frakes said he considered blaming his diet. Maybe it was beets, he mused, before realizing he hadn’t touched one in six years.

Frakes ultimately called his doctor, a decision that may have saved his bladder.

According to Narayanan, Frakes experienced what is clinically known as painless gross hematuria, or visible blood in the urine without accompanying pain.

“When it’s painless blood that you see with your eyes, that’s always a red flag,” the doctor said on the podcast.

While blood in the urine can stem from benign causes like urinary tract infections or kidney stones, painless visible hematuria is the most common symptom of bladder cancer. It always warrants an immediate urological evaluation, according to both Cleveland Clinic and the National Institutes of Health (NIH).

Days after finishing a fan convention, Frakes underwent an in-office cystoscopy, a quick procedure in which a thin camera examines the lining of the bladder. Inside, Narayanan spotted small, fern-like growths.

entertainment.title: Amanda Seyfrield Admits She ‘Told a Lot of People’ About Elizabeth Holmes Documentary
entertainment.summary: "How the hell did I manage to keep it under wraps?" the actress asked on The Tonight Show
entertainment.body:
Amanda Seyfried stopped by The Tonight Show to reflect on her experience making Elizabeth Holmes documentary You Can See Everything .

“It was never my intention to recreate Elizabeth Holmes ever again,” Seyfried noted to host Jimmy Fallon . She explained that Emma Stone connected her with the film’s co-director Nathan Fielder , who said he wanted to pick her brain about Holmes, who she had played in The Dropout . Initially, Fielder planned to film her watching some of the documentary footage he’d shot so far.

“It was fascinating,” Seyfried said, adding that “we kept organically deciding to do more things.” Fielder eventually convinced Seyfried to play Holmes again during reenactments in the film. “It was weird,” Seyfried said of returning to the character.

She said it was especially challenging because she couldn’t watch the documentary footage unless she was present on the set and the script was only accessible via “five-factor authentication” the night before. “I was so insecure about it,” Seyfried said. “ The Dropout is fiction based on real things. This is based on what we know.”

Seyfried added, “What an experience. I haven’t processed it fully because it was meta at a point.”

She also admitted that she had a hard time keeping her role a secret. “I’m the most indiscreet person I’ve ever met in my life,” Seyfried told Fallon. “How the hell did I manage to keep it under wraps? I told a lot of people. But I guess I could trust them all.”

Taylor Swift’s former music teacher is pushing back against Vanity Fair’s hit piece on the pop star , claiming her comments were taken out of context.

Sharon Luyben, who taught Swift, 36, in seventh and eighth grades at Wyomissing Area Junior-Senior High School in Pennsylvania, insisted that she had nothing but positive things to say about her former student.

“All I said were positive things,” the now-retired educator told TMZ on Tuesday, describing Swift as a “fabulous student.”

The longtime teacher, who also knew Swift’s parents through their church and the local community, said they were “very nice and active in our community.”

The Vanity Fair article, published Monday and written by May Jeong, was titled “The Mastermind” and featured just one comment from Luyben — one that challenged the “Shake It Off” singer’s recollection of being ostracized by classmates.

Swift recalled to Katie Couric in a 2009 interview that classmates would get up and move their lunch trays when she tried to sit with them.

entertainment.body:

The Dark Lord is at the height of his power after crafting the One Ring at the end of Episode 7 , and it's going to take a minor miracle to stop him... or is it?

All of the storylines this season race towards a seemingly inevitable battle that could possibly topple the balance of power in Middle-earth, as Galadriel (Morfydd Clark), Elrond (Robert Aramayo), and King Gil-Galad (Mark Ferguson) try to keep the Númenoreans from fleeing the impending war. Meanwhile, Gandalf (Daniel Weyman) desperately tries to turn Pallando (Ciarán Hinds) away from Sauron's grasp.

But while the Season 3 finale ominously threatens to spark the flame of war, it never really ignites. Instead, it takes a much more calculated approach — which might be a little disappointing for some audiences hoping to see Sauron and the elves battle for the soul of Middle-earth. It's a good thing Prime Video has already renewed "The Rings of Power" for Season 4 ! Let's unpack the last episode, and figure out what Sauron's smirk really means.

Prime Video Gandalf is finally at the forefront of the episode in Mordor this time after taking a back seat. The armies of Rhûn have amassed at Sauron's tower, and Khamûl (Zubin Varla) gives the wizard to the Dark Lord as a gift. Sure, Sauron already has one member of the Istari under his control, but why not have two? He tries to convince Gandalf to join him, and even offers to give him Middle-earth itself so it can be "cradled in your gentle hands," claiming that he also works for the Secret Fire in keeping the world on the right path. Sure, Sauron, sure. The villain even tempts Gandalf with a ring of his own... but the wizard whimsically declines: "None for me, thank you."

Almost instantly, he finds himself back in a cell and is joined by none other than Nori Brandyfoot! Yes, Markella Kavenagh reprises her role in a brief and not at all suspicious cameo... It's the Celeborn (Jamie Campbell Bower) kiss from Episode 6 all over again! She's Sauron in disguise, trying to trick Gandalf into joining him as a backwards way of protecting those he cares about. He almost falls for it but tricks Nori/Sauron with a classic "remember what your brother used to say?" Even though Nori didn't have a brother... You've got to try harder than that, Sauron.

Ezra Frech and Daniella Karagach shimmied off with the Len Goodman Mirrorball trophy after winning season 35 of ABC’s Dancing With The Stars .

In doing so, Frech, the two-time Paralympic gold medalist for Team U.S.A. in track and field, becomes the first amputee winner of the celebrity dance-off.

The finale episode on Tuesday night (Nov. 24) saw contestants compete in three rounds. First-up, the judges’ choice round, where each judge threw down the gauntlet by choosing the dance style for the final competitors. Next was the instant dance challenge, which meant the contestants needed to be fast learners, and quick on their feet. In an earlier interview published in The Hollywood Reporter , Frech said it would be “very, very special” to become the first amputee winner of DWTS . “Of course, getting the opportunity to make the finale, to win the show, to get to represent the disabled community in that way and become the first amputee to win Dancing With the Stars would be very, very special, and would mean a lot to myself and hopefully to all people with disabilities and the community as a whole,” he remarked.

After weeks of intense competition, the Season 35 champions of “Dancing With the Stars” are… Ezra Frech and Daniella Karagach!

The evening kicked off with the “Judges’ Choice” round, where judges Carrie Ann Inaba, Derek Hough and Bruno Tonioli challenged each finalist to recreate a dance style they performed earlier this season.

Disney/Eric McCandless Add TVLine on Google: Preferred Source Google Discover Who doesn't love a good Thanksgiving tradition? You've got the stuffing and mashed potatoes, you've got the Macy's parade... and, yep, you've got the "Dancing With the Stars" season finale, which typically falls just before Turkey Day. And much like the big meal coming later this week, Tuesday's "Dancing" finale kept us well-fed, offering up no less than three hours of competitive performances as the Mirrorball trophy awaited its newest owner.

Ahead of the season ender, we asked TVLine readers for their thoughts on who would win and who should win Season 35 of the ABC competition, and the polls were nailbiters: With just hours to go before the finale went live, Ezra Frech and Amber Glenn were neck-and-neck in the question of who would win (with Ezra beating Amber by just 0.2%!), while Amber narrowly edged out Ezra in the question of who should win.

And though our poll results indicated that Tatyana Ali, Maura Higgins, and Connor Wood had significantly lower chances of winning the Mirrorball, that's just a small sample of the "Dancing" viewership; Connor and Tatyana, though underdogs, have gotten plenty of love on social media for weeks, and Maura made an 11th-hour push for the big win in last week's semifinals , where she delivered a fantastic samba that's still circulating on this recapper's TikTok feed.

So, who emerged victorious in the end? K eep scrolling for our full recap of the finale's performances and results, then hit the comments with your thoughts on who won Season 35!

ABC First up was the Judges' Choice round, in which Carrie Ann Inaba, Derek Hough, and Bruno Tonioli challenged each couple to put a fresh spin on a style they'd performed earlier in the season, then visited rehearsals during the week to offer some constructive criticism.
